A study published in the Eastern Mediterranean Health Journal in 2004 examined morbidity patterns, focusing on infant and young child feeding practices and their association with diarrheal diseases in Indian children. The findings were detailed in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in 2020. 2. Research by Popkin et al. in 1990, published in Pediatrics, explored the relationship between breastfeeding and diarrheal morbidity, emphasizing the protective effects of breastfeeding against gastrointestinal infections. 3. Eaton-Evans and Dugdale (1987) investigated the impact of feeding methods and social factors on the incidence of diarrhea and vomiting in infants. Their findings were published in the Archives of Disease in Childhood. 4. Kalanda et al. (2006) studied breastfeeding and complementary feeding practices in Malawian infants, analyzing their effects on growth and morbidity. This research was published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 5. Mondal et al. (1996) examined the occurrence of diarrheal diseases in relation to infant feeding practices in a rural community in West Bengal, India. The study was published in Acta Paediatrica. 6. English et al. (2019) conducted a systematic review on the timing of introducing complementary foods and beverages, assessing their impact on growth, body size, and composition. The findings were published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 7. Bainbridge (1996) conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) in Ohio, USA, comparing cereal-fed infants with formula-fed infants. Outcomes included weight, length, skinfold thickness, and various biochemical markers. 8. Dewey (1998, 2004) conducted RCTs in Honduras, focusing on breastfeeding practices and their effects on lactational amenorrhea, energy intake, growth, and micronutrient levels in infants. 9. Gupta (2017) conducted an RCT in India comparing complementary feeding at 4 months versus 6 months in preterm and small-for-gestational-age infants. Outcomes included growth, neurodevelopment, and dietary diversity. 10. Jonsdottir (2014) conducted an RCT in Iceland comparing exclusive breastfeeding with complementary feeding. Outcomes included developmental milestones, growth parameters, and iron status. 11. Marriott (2003) conducted an RCT in the United Kingdom on preterm infants, comparing complementary feeding after 3 months versus 4 months. Outcomes included growth velocities, energy intake, and iron status. 12. Perkin (2018) conducted an RCT in the United Kingdom comparing early (3 months) versus standard (6 months) complementary feeding. Outcomes included sleep patterns and allergy development. 13. Skjerven (2020) conducted an RCT in Norway and Sweden, examining the effects of early complementary feeding on atopic dermatitis and hospitalization rates. 14.
